title: Consistency Training Can Entrench Misalignment
claim: Enforcing agreement across perturbations can either filter out or entrench latent misalignment, depending on which behavioral mode dominates the consensus.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right, big arrows branching into two outcome boxes
description: A left-to-right schematic in three rounded panels. The left gray panel, 'Internal LLM State', shows a dashed circle filled with blue dots (benign capabilities) and red dots (latent misalignment), with an LLM robot icon and colored labels with examples such as helpfulness, sycophancy and reward hacking. A big blue arrow leads to the middle blue panel, 'Consistency Training'. It has a short italic definition and a robot icon fanning out to three perturbation icons: a lightning bolt, a moon and a heart. These are labeled τ1 to τ3, with the caption 'Seven consistency methods evaluated'. Two arrows then split, green up and orange down. They lead to a green 'Outcome A: Suppression' panel, where mostly blue dots sit under a shield with a checkmark and the red dots are crossed out. They also lead to an orange 'Outcome B: Amplification' panel, where red dots dominate under a warning triangle. The eye goes first to the colored dot clouds and the branching arrows.
caption: Consistency non-neutrality hypothesis. Language models contain both aligned (blue) and misaligned (red) behavioral modes. Consistency training enforces agreement across perturbations τ (e.g., different sampling strategies, prompt framings, or decoding methods). Two non-neutral outcomes are possible: suppression, where aligned behavior dominates the consensus and misalignment is reduced; or amplification, where misaligned behavior is reinforced and consistency solidifies unwanted goals.
abstract: Consistency training encourages a model to produce similar outputs across related inputs or sampling procedures. Such methods are simple, scalable, and largely label-free, but their effects on model alignment remain poorly understood. Could the self-bootstrapping nature of these methods amplify undesired behavior in models? We test seven consistency training methods on 108 model organisms: open-source models (7B--70B) fine-tuned to exhibit various forms of controlled misaligned behavior. We find that outcomes vary significantly: consistency training generally suppresses reward hacking and emergent misalignment but amplifies sycophancy. We present evidence that distribution shifts induced by the consistency labeling process, rather than variation in the selection operators, may be the primary driver of systematic alignment effects. Finally, we present a unifying theoretical framework to derive conditions under which consistency training will amplify or suppress misalignment. In total, our study establishes that consistency training is not alignment-neutral, and that its use in critical systems should be carefully audited.
